checkpoints: Mass-assignment happens because the raw request body is assigned straight onto the entity, so an extra field like isAdmin:true lands in the DB exactly like any legitimate field — the danger is the unfiltered assignment path, not the field itself.

The fix is an allowlist: the input contract declares the fields that are permitted, and the boundary strips or rejects everything outside that list, defeating the attack by construction no matter what new field a client invents.
A denylist is the fragile inverse — it only survives until someone adds a new sensitive column and forgets to update the block-list, which is guaranteed to happen eventually.
Stripping unrecognized fields is forgiving (good for a public API tolerating sloppy clients), but a typoed field then silently does nothing while the client believes the update succeeded.
Rejecting explicitly with an error is fail-fast and better during integration and for write endpoints, since silence there only hides bugs rather than helping anyone.

The corollary: never reuse the persistence entity as the input DTO, since the entity exposes internal columns and reopens the exact mass-assignment hole the allowlist just closed — the DTO must always be a separate boundary artifact.
Two choke points exist because there are only two possible output branches — a returned value (success) and a thrown exception (error) — so centralizing exactly there covers every response.
Centralizing yields one root shape (one parsing path for the client) and one file to change when the contract evolves, instead of hunting through every handler.
Handlers are freed to do pure business logic — return data or throw a meaningful exception — with no formatting concern.
The error boundary doubles as the security border: known errors pass through with their real status and message, while unknown errors degrade to a generic 500.
Stack traces, PII, and internal messages are logged server-side only and never serialized back to the client.

Traceability comes from timestamp + path + typed details (a field-error array for validation, resource/id for not-found), turning the same shape into something machine-actionable and log-joinable for investigating production incidents.

Honest trade-off: wrapping adds a layer of indirection and doesn't fit a team already standardized on bare resource bodies or RFC 7807 problem-details — the success envelope shape is negotiable per team, but the single centralized catch-all error boundary is not.
In an UpdateUserDto where every field is marked optional, a client that omits a field causes that field to arrive at the handler as `undefined`, not as something the handler can treat as "skip this."

Assigning a payload field directly onto the entity row without checking whether it was actually present applies full-replace semantics to a route meant to only touch what changed — the omitted field gets overwritten with `undefined`, and the ORM persists that as `null`, wiping previously stored data.

PUT and PATCH differ in write scope: PUT is a full replacement where the client sends the complete representation and the server can assign every field directly, while PATCH is a partial update where the server must write only the fields present in the payload and leave everything else untouched.

The fix is a per-field presence check before assignment — e.g. `if (payload.name !== undefined) row.name = payload.name` — so a field absent from the payload keeps its previously stored value instead of being cleared.

Adding a "keep the old value if the field is absent" fallback to a genuine PUT handler is the mirror-image bug: it lets omitted fields silently survive a request that is contractually supposed to overwrite the whole resource, breaking PUT's replace-everything guarantee.

Verifying the fix requires checking both directions independently: PATCH with a partial body leaves the untouched field unchanged, PUT with a full body overwrites every field, and resending that same PUT payload again converges the resource to the same state, which is the idempotency property both PUT and PATCH are expected to have.

The presence-check strategy is representation-dependent: an `!== undefined`/null check works when the language distinguishes "absent" from "a real value," but in languages where an absent field arrives as a zero-value (e.g. an empty string in Go), the same strategy needs a different signal — a pointer type or an explicit presence map — to distinguish "not sent" from "sent as empty."

A plain undefined/null presence check cannot distinguish "field was never sent" from "field was sent as null/empty specifically to clear it" — supporting an intentional clear operation requires an extra signal beyond simple presence checking, such as a sentinel value or a separate "fields to clear" list.

Two error shapes coming out of the same API for what is conceptually the same kind of failure (an error) usually means two different code paths are handling errors, not one - the discriminator is a property of how each error is routed, not randomness or client-side parsing.

A parameterized `@Catch(HttpException)` scopes a filter to only intercept exceptions that are instances of that specific type - it does not act as a global safety net for everything an application can throw.

A plain `throw new Error("boom")` is not an instance of `HttpException`, so it never matches a filter scoped with `@Catch(HttpException)` and is never routed to that filter at all, regardless of the filter being registered globally.

An exception that bypasses a type-scoped filter falls straight through to the framework's own built-in default exception handler, which builds its own response body in a different shape and, depending on configuration, can surface the raw error message or a stack trace directly to the client.

Making the catch registration unconditional (a parameterless `@Catch()`) turns the filter into a true catch-all so no exception type can structurally bypass it, closing the gap that let plain runtime errors slip through.

Once the filter is a catch-all, it must branch internally: when the caught value is an `HttpException`, its real status and message are preserved and returned as before; otherwise the response is hardcoded to a generic 500 with a generic message, while the actual exception and its stack trace are logged server-side only, never included in the response body.

An exception filter functions as the single border deciding what error information leaves the system, so preventing leaks has to be a structural property of that boundary's scope rather than a hope that every handler always throws a recognized, deliberately-shaped error.

Correctness after the fix is confirmed by three checks together: the previously-leaking endpoint now returns the same envelope shape with a generic message and no internal string; a genuine `HttpException` such as a 404 still returns its original status and details unchanged; and the real error plus its stack trace still appears in server logs, showing nothing was silently swallowed - only hidden from the client.

Copying an entire raw request body directly onto a persistence entity (mass assignment) lets a client set fields the API never intended to accept — for example flipping an `isAdmin` flag to true through one extra key in the payload — which is a privilege-escalation vulnerability, not a cosmetic issue.

The fix for mass assignment is a declared boundary contract — a DTO listing only the fields the endpoint is meant to accept — enforced as an allowlist (e.g. a validation pipe configured with `whitelist`/`forbidNonWhitelisted`) so unknown fields are stripped or the whole request is rejected before it ever reaches the persistence layer.

Reusing the persistence entity itself as the input type merges the wire contract with the storage shape, so any column added later for internal bookkeeping (like an admin flag) automatically becomes a client-writable input field.

Manual inline validation — scattered if-statements invented per handler — drifts over time, tends to miss real rules such as email format checking, and produces inconsistent, ad hoc error messages across different endpoints.

Declarative validation (decorators such as `@IsEmail`, `@MinLength`, `@Min`) combined with one global validation layer applied to every route produces consistent, structured error responses and removes the need to hand-roll checks per handler.

A nested object field, such as an address, is persisted with no deep validation unless the contract explicitly declares nested validation for it, so an invalid nested value is silently stored instead of surfacing an error with a specific field path like `address.zip`.

A query parameter that looks numeric is still a string on the wire; without explicit type coercion, a comparison such as `age >= minAge` compares a number against a string and can silently misbehave instead of throwing an error.

Verifying a fix for these problems means confirming that an unexpected extra field is rejected or stripped rather than persisted, that a bad nested field returns an error carrying its correct nested path, that a numeric-looking query parameter now compares correctly, and that a previously valid payload still behaves exactly as before.
A spinner hides the wait but doesn't shorten it — the real fix must be architectural, not cosmetic.
The core problem is bundling the entire response into one reply instead of pushing each part the moment it's produced.
With SSE the server holds the connection open, frames each token as an event, and writes and flushes it immediately so the client renders incrementally from the first token.

Specific headers (event-stream content type, no-cache/no-transform, immediate header flush) form the contract that keeps proxies from buffering — buffering anywhere reintroduces the original 'wait then get one blob' behavior.
Because a stream doesn't end itself the way a returned response does, the client can't tell from a closed socket alone whether it finished or broke — completion must become an explicit event.
A done event (carrying tokenCount) is the explicit success signal, letting the client verify it received every token rather than guess.
A unified error envelope {code, message} signals a mid-flight break, and nothing is emitted after a client abort.
This makes the client slightly more complex (handling multiple event types) but it always knows the stream's true state instead of guessing from a closed connection.

Stuffing every document into the prompt blows the context limit and burns tokens on content irrelevant to the question, while fine-tuning is expensive, slow to update, and the model can still hallucinate on out-of-scope questions.
RAG solves this by keeping knowledge outside the model, in a vector store, rather than baking it into weights or cramming it into context.
At ingest time, each document is embedded and stored (e.g. a vector column in pgvector).
At query time, the question must be embedded with the exact same embedder used for the documents — mandatory, because with a different embedder the distance between vectors becomes meaningless.
The top-k nearest chunks by cosine similarity are retrieved directly inside the database.
Only the retrieved chunks are placed into the prompt (augmentation), anchoring the answer in real documents rather than the model's memory.
The response carries citations (the exact ids of chunks used), making it traceable.
The system is near-instant to update — just add or edit documents, no retraining needed.

In a prompt-safety pipeline, redacting PII before the injection scanner runs wastes redaction work on prompts that are about to be blocked anyway, and it makes the block decision incidentally depend on the redaction step having executed first — a dependency that should not exist. The injection scan should run first, against the raw prompt, before any redaction happens.

Wrapping the injection-scanner call in a try/catch that logs a warning and then calls the LLM provider anyway on any exception is a fail-open design: the exact moment the scanner is broken or throws is the moment the entire safety gate silently becomes a pass-through, forwarding the raw, unredacted prompt straight to the provider.

Of the violations in such a pipeline, the fail-open catch around the scanner is the most severe because it is silent and total — any runtime exception converts the whole gate into a bypass, and a log line like "scanner failed, continuing" reads as a benign warning rather than signaling that the safety layer just failed, so no one gets paged for it.

Because redaction runs before the scan, a scanner failure forwards a prompt that has already been redacted, which makes the response look "safe-ish" even though the actual security control — injection detection — never ran at all; the two violations compound each other.

Writing the full raw prompt into the audit log when a request is blocked, "for debugging," copies any PII that prompt contains into every log aggregator and retention policy that engineers with log access can reach — a second, unintended exposure of the exact data the pipeline exists to protect, even though nothing left the process to an external provider.

A fail-closed fix means any exception during the scan step must result in a blocked response (or be rethrown to a global filter that returns an error status), never a fallthrough to the provider call — "I don't know if this is safe" has to be treated the same as "this is unsafe," not the same as "this is safe."

Audit logging on a blocked decision should record only the decision and evidence — such as the matched finding kinds — never the raw prompt text; on a successful forward, only the already-redacted prompt should be logged, never the original raw input.

Proving such a fix requires tests showing: a prompt containing both an injection phrase and PII is blocked with zero calls to the provider and no redaction warning, proving order; forcing the scanner to throw results in a blocked response and never a forwarded one, proving fail-closed behavior; and captured log output for both a block and a forward never contains the raw PII substring from the input, proving the log boundary holds.

Selecting every row from `documents` with no `ORDER BY` and no `LIMIT` forces the full table — id, content, and every embedding vector — to be pulled out of Postgres and shipped over the wire on each retrieval call.

Computing `cosineSimilarity` in application code once per row is an O(n) scan across the entire corpus for every single query, and sorting all of those scored rows in memory before slicing the top 3 wastes work on rows that get thrown away.

This pattern is invisible at a handful of seed documents because the data volume and scan cost are both trivial, but it degrades badly as the corpus grows into the hundreds of thousands of chunks — the LLM call is not the bottleneck, the network transfer and the app-side scan are.

The first-stage fix is to move the nearest-neighbour search into the database itself: query with `ORDER BY embedding <=> $1::vector LIMIT $2` using pgvector's cosine-distance operator, so Postgres does the ranking and only the top-k rows ever cross the wire.

The similarity-to-score conversion (`1 - distance`) and the `SIMILARITY_THRESHOLD` filter should still be applied, but only to the k rows the database returns, not to the whole corpus — the app-side `cosineSimilarity` and `parseVectorLiteral` helpers drop out of the request path entirely once the query does the work.

An approximate nearest-neighbour index such as HNSW or IVFFlat should only be introduced once the exact in-database scan itself becomes the bottleneck at very large scale — it is a second-stage optimization, not an automatic first move.

Adding an ANN index trades exactness for speed: the neighbours returned become approximate rather than guaranteed top-k, so the recall loss versus the latency gain is a judged trade-off rather than a free win.

Verifying the change means measuring p95 query latency before and after at a realistic corpus size, running `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` to confirm the query plan actually uses the index once one exists, checking retrieval quality hasn't silently regressed by comparing approximate results against an exact scan on a sample of queries, and re-running the grounded and fallback end-to-end flows to confirm answers still cite the right chunks.

User-perceived latency in a streaming response is governed by time-to-first-token, not total generation time — the two are independent, and a fix that shortens total generation time without moving the first byte earlier does nothing for perceived latency.

Setting `Content-Type: text/event-stream` and shaping each event correctly makes an endpoint look like it streams, but the actual guarantee of streaming is that bytes cross the socket as each token is produced — correct framing and early delivery are separate properties, and only the second one fixes a blank-screen wait.

Pushing each formatted token into an in-memory array (or string) inside a `for await` loop and calling `res.write` only once after the loop exits collapses time-to-first-token to the full generation duration, because nothing reaches the client until every token has already been generated.

A client's request status can flip to 'streaming' the instant the HTTP response opens, independent of whether the server has written any data yet — so status alone does not prove data is arriving, and a blank screen with status already 'streaming' points at server-side buffering rather than a client-side issue.

Fixing the in-memory accumulation bug is not sufficient on its own: headers set via `setHeader` are not guaranteed to reach the client until the first write or an explicit flush, so calling `res.flushHeaders()` right after setting headers is needed for the client to see the connection open before the first token arrives.

Without a `Cache-Control: no-cache, no-transform` response header (and, behind nginx specifically, `X-Accel-Buffering: no`), an intermediate reverse proxy or CDN is free to buffer correctly-flushed per-token writes and release them together later — so the server-side fix and the anti-buffering header are two independent, both-required fixes for the same symptom.

The correct fix moves the write inside the loop: each token is written and flushed to the response the moment it is produced, with no accumulating array or string kept — only a running counter is needed to report the total token count in the terminal 'done' event.

Verifying a streaming fix requires more than reading the code: asserting that response output grows while status is still 'streaming', measuring time-to-first-token before and after the fix, and re-running that check through the actual reverse proxy or CDN in front of the service — since a local request bypasses proxy-level buffering and cannot reveal it.
